input:
In this work, the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures, in order to establish how the rate of reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant was found to be k = 0.085 s-1. At 340 K, by contrast, k = 1.311 s-1, this second value having been computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 58 kJ mol-1 and being presented here as a derived value rather than as a direct measurement.

Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which gives a reasonable indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. It can be seen that the value at 340 K stands 15.4 times the value at 300 K, so that the rate constant increases very steeply indeed over what is a relatively modest interval of temperature, a behaviour that is consistent with the size of the activation energy involved. It is perhaps worth noting that, because the higher-temperature value is derived rather than measured, it depends jointly on the quality of the lower-temperature measurement and on the activation energy that has been adopted.

Above 340 K, difficulties were encountered because the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. This is essentially a practical limitation of the experimental procedure, in that samples taken at higher temperatures lost solvent before they could be analysed, and any value extracted from them would have been unreliable.
target:
The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.085 s-1. At 340 K, k = 1.311 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 58 kJ mol-1 as a derived value.

Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The triplicate measurement fixes the precision of the measured value at the lower temperature, and the derived value at the higher temperature is computed from that measured base through the Arrhenius relation, so its reliability rests on the measured value and on the activation energy together. The value at 340 K stands 15.4 times the value at 300 K: across the interval the rate constant rises steeply, and the size of the rise is the size the activation energy produces over this temperature span for a reaction of this order. A change in either input, the measured rate constant or the activation energy, would move the derived value in proportion, and the reported figure should be read with that dependence in view.

Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The evaporation is a limit of the measurement, not a property of the reaction: samples taken at higher temperatures lost solvent before analysis, and a rate constant computed from them would describe the sampling failure rather than the kinetics. The reported results therefore cover the two stated temperatures and the interval between them, and the Arrhenius computation is not extended past the point where the measurement itself failed.
